newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria holds out for economic reforms on own terms.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria holds out for economic reforms on own terms.

text.p: Nigeria's military rulers showed they would not bend to outside pressure for change when they delayed economic reforms which were widely expected in the 1997 budget announced at the weekend.

Investors looking for a clear statement from military ruler General Sani Abacha that loss-making but potentially profitable state firms would be up for sale to attract badly-needed funds only got a promise that a committee would be set up to study privatisation.

"This government is uncomfortable about anything that makes them feel they are pandering to foreigners," said Chuka Okafor, a banker. "They know privatisation is the key to unlocking the economy but they will do it only on their own terms."

"Whatever we do, we will do it because we want to and are convinced that we should and not because anyone wants us to," said finance minister Anthony Ani at a budget briefing in the capital Abuja on Monday.

Nigeria has been mired in political crisis since 1993 when a previous army government annulled a presidential poll that should have restored democracy. It is now shunned by its traditional Western partners because of human rights abuses and lack of democracy.
Ani first raised the prospect of privatising Nigerian enterprises at a World Bank conference in Washington last year.
It attracted interest from some of the six multinationals that pump Nigeria's crude oil under joint venture arrangements which the country is finding difficult to sustain financially.

Ani said he did not like the joint ventures under which Nigeria has equity of up to 60 percent in the multinationals' local subsidiaries and has to fund their activities to that level through cash-calls, which for 1997 amount to $2.05 billion.
By selling these equity stakes Nigeria could raise billions of dollars to invest in developing the nation while also freeing itself of the burden of paying cash-calls.
Since the mid-1990s, Nigeria has signed only what are called production sharing contracts under which oil companies finance explorations and recoup their costs if oil is struck.
"The truth is that Nigeria knows joint ventures are out of date and will not enter into such arrangements any more," said Rashid Ayeni, a consultant oil engineer.
According to finance ministry officials some of the studies to be conducted are to determine the value of Nigerian state enterprises so that they will not be sold at a discount.
Many businessmen at the Abuja briefing were disappointed that a timetable of privatisation had not been announced but they thought this had to happen sooner rather than later.

"It is not whether we have to privatise. We have no choice and until that happens we are still not talking the language the outside world understands," said a member of Abacha's Vision 2010 committee who would not be named.
The committee is charged with planning how to make resource-rich Nigeria a prosperous nation by 2010, the year when the West African nation will have been independent for 50 years.
The 1997 budget announced far-reaching banking reforms and pumped money into social sectors which government said would improve the lives of the 100 million people in Africa's most populous nation.

Under-capitalised banks will be liquidated after March, more people will be prosecuted for corruption, money will be spent on restoring infrastructure and a new programme to set up cottage industries in rural areas will commence.

"What we want is a black country that will emerge with a strong economy to play a role internationally," said information minister Walter Ofonagoro. "Foreign firms who left will be competing to come back into what is becoming a fast-growing economy."
Gross domestic product growth is expected to be 5.5 percent in 1997 compared with 3.25 percent in 1996. Inflation is set to fall to 15 percent in 1997 from 28 percent at the end of 1996.

But nagging political problems remain including the detention since 1994 of Moshood Abiola, the presumed winner of the annulled poll. Recently bomb attacks linked to the political crisis have killed three soldiers and wounded several dozen others.
